headline: Inside the Network of Cameras Reading America’s License Plates
deck: Volunteers have mapped more than {{mappedFlock|k}} cameras made by one company, Flock Safety. Public records show who can search what they capture, how long it is kept and what comes of it.
intro: On poles at intersections, in store parking lots and along state highways, small cameras photograph the rear of passing cars. Most are made by Flock Safety, an Atlanta company that provides them for an annual fee to police departments, homeowner associations and businesses, and that says its cameras make [more than 20 billion scans a month](src:nbc-flock-2025).

Flock does not publish a map of its cameras. Volunteers have been recording them, one at a time, on [OpenStreetMap](src:deflock-tiles-2026), the map anyone can edit. The map below uses the copy published by DeFlock, an [anti-surveillance group](src:texastribune-2026) that tracks the company’s cameras.

map.alt: A map of the United States made of dots, one for each license plate reader recorded on OpenStreetMap; the dots are densest along highways and around cities in the South, the Midwest, Texas and California.

steps.text: Each dot is a license plate reader that volunteers have mapped. As of {{snapshot|date}}, there were {{mappedTotal}}.
Flock made about four in five of them, shown in orange. The rest, in gray, come from companies including Motorola Solutions, Genetec and Axis Communications.

Measured against population, Flock’s cameras are most common in the South, with {{regions.2.rate}} for every 100,000 residents, and least common in the Northeast, with {{regions.0.rate}}. Volunteers have mapped none in {{countiesNone.count}} counties, home to about {{countiesNone.popShare|pct}} percent of Americans; {{countiesNoneTop.0.name}}, {{countiesNoneTop.1.name}}, {{countiesNoneTop.2.name}} and {{countiesNoneTop.3.name}} have the most such counties.
Georgia, where Flock is based, has the most per resident: {{topState.rate}} mapped Flock cameras for every 100,000 people, {{topState.ratio}} times the national rate.

In Fulton County, which includes most of Atlanta, volunteers have mapped {{topBigCounty.flock}} Flock cameras, about {{topBigCounty.rate|round}} for every 100,000 residents, the highest rate of any county with a million or more people.

blocks.p: The map is a record of what volunteers have seen, not an official inventory. Where cities publish their own counts, the mapped number can be higher, because it includes cameras that other owners run inside city limits, or lower, where mapping has not caught up. In Oakland, Calif., volunteers have mapped {{completeness.Oakland.mapped}} Flock cameras inside the city line; the Police Department reported [290 of its own](src:oakland-pac-2026), and {{oaklandChp.count}} of the mapped cameras are tagged as run by the California Highway Patrol.

Flock says it operates in [more than 6,000 communities in 49 states](src:wikipedia-flock). Volunteers have mapped {{usFlock}} Flock cameras in the 50 states and the District of Columbia, about {{usRate|round}} for every 100,000 residents.

California and Texas have the most, {{mostStates.0.flock}} and {{mostStates.1.flock}}. Per resident, Georgia leads, followed by Ohio, Texas, Indiana and Alabama. New Hampshire has the fewest per resident: {{bottomStates.0.flock}} mapped cameras, {{bottomStates.0.rate}} for every 100,000 people.

Police departments are not the only customers. Volunteers have recorded who runs {{operatorsNamed.count}} of the mapped Flock cameras, {{operatorsNamed.share}} percent of them. Of those, {{operatorsPolice.share}} percent are listed as run by police or sheriffs and {{operatorsRetail.share}} percent by retailers and shopping centers.

The largest named operators are Lowe’s, with {{topOperators.0.count}} mapped cameras, and Home Depot, with {{topOperators.1.count}}. This year, shareholder proposals asked both companies to report on the privacy risks of sharing customer data, including images from the cameras in their parking lots. Both boards [recommended voting no](src:prospect-retail-2026). At the annual meetings in May, the proposals won 8.9 percent of the votes cast at [Home Depot](src:homedepot-8k-2026) and 9.1 percent at [Lowe’s](src:lowes-8k-2026).
The cameras are set off by [motion](src:flock-flex-datasheet). When a vehicle passes, one takes [six to 12 still photographs](src:jalopnik-speed) of its rear, lit at night by an infrared array.

Software reads the plate and its state. It also describes the vehicle — its make, type and color, and features such as roof racks, bumper stickers and decals — in what Flock calls a [Vehicle Fingerprint](src:flock-deck-2023). The camera adds the time, its GPS position and its own identifier, and [Flock’s policy](src:flock-lpr-policy) says the plate and vehicle images are then transferred to the company’s servers.

Each read travels over a cellular connection to Flock’s servers on [Amazon Web Services](src:flock-arch-2024), where it is stored and indexed for search. Plates are checked against hot lists: the F.B.I.’s National Crime Information Center and the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children, [Flock’s policy](src:flock-lpr-policy) says, as well as [Amber Alerts and custom lists](src:flock-flex-datasheet) that agencies write themselves.

When a plate matches, an alert with the photo, the plate and the camera’s location reaches officers in [10 to 15 seconds on average](src:flock-flex-datasheet), according to Flock. The American Civil Liberties Union found that the F.B.I.’s list reaches the cameras only [twice a day](src:aclu-2022), so a plate taken off it can keep setting off alerts for up to 12 hours.

How long the pictures are kept depends on settings and state law. On Aug. 13, 2026, Flock [made seven days its default](src:flock-guardrails-2026) for new customers, down from 30; existing customers keep the periods they had set. [Virginia](src:va-code-2-2-5517) and [Washington](src:wa-sb6002-2026) require deletion after 21 days unless the data is needed for an investigation, and California limits its Highway Patrol to [60](src:ca-sb34). A feature called Evidence Mode keeps data tied to an investigation, with [no published limit](src:aclu-guardrails).

Officers at a customer agency can search the reads by plate, by a description of the vehicle or with a written prompt, across their own cameras and those of agencies that share with them. Agencies can also join a national lookup; about 75 percent of Flock’s law enforcement customers had joined, [the company told Congress](src:wyden-ftc-2025) in August 2025.

Each search adds a row to an audit log, with a reason the officer types. Logs released under public records laws show how far one search can reach. On May 9, 2025, the sheriff’s office in Johnson County, Tex., searched a week of reads from 17,684 cameras in 1,295 networks, then a month of reads from 83,345 cameras in 6,809 networks. Both searches logged the same reason, according to [records published by the Electronic Frontier Foundation](src:eff-texas-2025), a digital rights group.
In a review of 12 million searches, the foundation found that about [one in five](src:eff-protesters-2025) gave a generic reason such as “investigation.”

Few agencies publish what their cameras lead to. Oakland’s Police Department publishes one of the fullest accounts. In 2025, its 290 Flock cameras recorded 638,747,333 plate reads, counting a plate each time it passed, and produced 1,099,837 alerts, about one for every 580 reads. Most of the alerts, 653,566, were for stolen plates or stolen vehicles, types the department [kept switched off](src:oakland-pac-2026) because it lacked the staff to respond.

Other departments count different steps, over different periods and with different definitions. In Los Angeles, the Police Commission’s inspector general counted [210.6 million reads](src:lapd-oig-2026) in two months from all of the department’s readers. Its in-car readers alone produced 50,183 alerts; 337 led to the recovery of a stolen vehicle, and 68 to stops that ended in 74 arrests.

Flock says its technology [supported about a million investigations](src:flock-impact-2026) in 2025. The figure comes from a survey of about 700 agencies, and the company calls its results “directional estimates rather than audited totals.”

The most detailed independent test so far is a working paper by two University of South Carolina criminologists, Scott M. Mourtgos and Ian T. Adams, who used deployment records that [Flock supplied](src:flock-study-2026); the company says it did not fund the work. Comparing 216 agencies that adopted the cameras with 3,108 that did not, they estimated that reported vehicle thefts [fell 11 percent](src:mourtgos-adams-2026) in the year after an agency’s first camera went live. They also estimated that the share of thefts cleared by an arrest, 7.4 percent in the year before, rose by about 16 percent of that level — roughly one more cleared theft in every 100 — though the rise began in the three months before the cameras went live, which the authors say weakens the link to the cameras.

The 11 percent estimate gives more weight to agencies that had more thefts before the cameras arrived. Weighted by population, or with every agency-month counted equally, the paper’s appendix shows no change that can be told apart from zero, a point the Institute for Justice, a libertarian law firm that [sued Norfolk, Va., over its Flock cameras](src:ij-norfolk), [made in September](src:reason-flock-study-2026). The authors say their main estimate describes the places that carry most of the thefts rather than a uniform effect. The paper has not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

An alert means that a camera’s reading of a plate matched an entry on a list. Records from three places show three ways that match can be wrong. Only one of them, Roseville, Calif., involves Flock cameras, and each measures its errors against a different total.

Customers pay a yearly fee that covers the camera, pole, solar panel, cellular data and software, and Flock [keeps ownership of the hardware](src:richland-agreement-2023). The list price is [$3,000 per camera per year](src:flock-catalog-2024), up from $2,500 before Jan. 1, 2024.

Contracts and quotes from [2022](src:richland-agreement-2023) and [2023](src:indio-2023) list a one-time installation fee of $350 to $650 a camera, or $150 to mount one on existing infrastructure. When a customer changes its plan after it is agreed, Flock’s 2026 schedule charges [$1,000 to $1,250](src:flock-fee-schedule) to install a camera and $350 to $5,000 to move one.

The largest public contracts run to millions of dollars. The Texas Department of Public Safety approved a [$26 million contract](src:texastribune-2026) in 2025; Johnson City, Tenn., approved [$8.1 million over 10 years](src:johnsoncity-2025).

This year some governments added cameras or renewed contracts while others ended, paused or restricted them, and Flock changed its own defaults. In Texas, after the governor paused state funding in August, The Texas Tribune counted [at least 14 cities and counties](src:texastribune-unplugged-2026) that had switched off more than 900 cameras. Dallas, which had said it would switch off the cameras paid for with state grants, said on Sept. 30 that they would [stay on for at least 90 days](src:fox4-dallas-2026); The Texas Tribune reported that Flock had [paused the city’s payments](src:texastribune-reprieve-2026) for them.

Finding Flock, an independent project that documents the cameras and [says it writes](src:findingflock-about) in “a neutral, data-journalism voice,” lists [45 decisions](src:findingflock-cancellations) from August 2025 to September 2026 to cancel, pause, deactivate, reject or not renew a contract, and says its list is not complete. A Flock spokesperson [said in August](src:kare11-flock-2026) that new city partnerships had outpaced nonrenewals “by approximately seven to one” so far this year, without giving the numbers. Sacra, a firm that estimates private companies’ revenue, put Flock’s annual recurring revenue at [about $450 million](src:sacra-flock) in October 2025 and $500 million in March 2026.

The map keeps changing, too. In the week before {{snapshot|date}}, volunteers added at least {{addedLastWeek.flock}} Flock cameras to it. In Windsor, Conn., where the council voted in July to keep the town’s cameras off, a mapper [deleted 14 of them](src:osm-windsor-2026) on Oct. 8, noting that each had been removed, “presumably” because the town had canceled its contract.
Each part of this story has a page with the full record: every figure, table and source.

Camera locations are OpenStreetMap nodes tagged as license plate readers, as served by [DeFlock’s hourly map tiles](src:deflock-tiles-2026), read on {{snapshot|date}}, and pinned with a checksum. Each was assigned to a county with the Census Bureau’s [2024 boundary files](src:census-boundaries-2024) and compared with [Vintage 2024 population estimates](src:census-pop-2024). Rates cover the 50 states and the District of Columbia; the national total of {{mappedFlock}} Flock cameras also includes {{outsideStates}} in Puerto Rico and elsewhere.

“Mapped” means recorded by volunteers. A camera nobody has tagged is missing, a removed camera can remain until someone deletes it, and a make or operator is known only when a mapper added it. DeFlock, whose copy of the map is used here, campaigns against the cameras; the records themselves are on OpenStreetMap, where anyone can check or correct them.

Outcome figures come from the agencies’ own reports and audits, quoted with their definitions and periods; they are not combined across agencies. Every number on this page is listed with its source in the project’s [fact-check ledger](https://github.com/realvivek/Flock/blob/main/docs/fact-check.md), and the counts are available as files: [cameras by state](data/story/cameras-by-state.csv), [by county](data/story/cameras-by-county.csv) and the [operator classes](data/story/operator-classes.csv).

Camera positions © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License. Population and boundaries: U.S. Census Bureau. This page does not describe ways to avoid or disable the cameras.

notes: Population estimates for July 1, 2024. Rates cover the 50 states and D.C.; the national total also counts {{outsideStates}} Flock cameras outside them, most in Puerto Rico.

notes: Counties in Connecticut are its nine planning regions, as the Census Bureau now reports them.

operators.title: Where an operator is recorded, most are police or sheriffs
operators.sub: Mapped Flock cameras by the type of operator volunteers recorded
notes: Operator names with 10 or more cameras were classified by hand, the rest by keyword; the classification is published with the data. The counts include the {{outsideStates}} mapped Flock cameras outside the 50 states and D.C.

read.title: Each read records more than the plate
read.sub: The fields a Flock camera records for a passing vehicle
notes: Illustration. The vehicle details are those Flock lists in a 2020 announcement and a 2023 sales presentation; The Texas Tribune reported that the cameras also record dents.

ruler.title: Seconds to an alert, days to deletion
ruler.sub: Time from the moment a plate is read, on a logarithmic scale
notes: No figure is published for the upload. Seven days is Flock’s default for new customers; existing customers keep the periods they set. As of Oct. 8, 2026, Flock’s Myths and Facts page still gives 30 days as the default. The state limits allow longer retention for data needed in an investigation.

audit.title: One search, 83,345 cameras
audit.sub: Audit log entries for two searches by the Johnson County, Tex., Sheriff’s Office on May 9, 2025, and three accounts of them
notes: As documented by the Electronic Frontier Foundation from the published logs; both entries carried the case number of the office’s death investigation.

oakland.title: In Oakland, one alert for every 580 reads
oakland.sub: Plate reads and alerts from the Police Department’s 290 Flock cameras in 2025; each square’s area is proportional to the count
notes: Alerts for stolen plates and stolen vehicles were generated but not sent to officers. A success story can record more than one result; outside agencies that search Oakland’s cameras do not always report theirs, and the department cannot see their records. The report does not explain why its two totals of vehicles and guns differ.

ladder.title: Alerts run from hundreds to tens of thousands; arrests, in the dozens
ladder.sub: Counts from each department’s report or audit, on a logarithmic scale
notes: Definitions differ: Nashville counted only hits an employee verified; Columbia counts cases cleared by arrest; Los Angeles’s reads are from all its readers, its alerts and outcomes from Axon readers in patrol cars. Periods differ. The figures are not a ranking.

evidence.title: Whether thefts fell depends on how agencies are weighted
evidence.sub: Estimated change in reported vehicle thefts in the year after an agency’s first Flock camera went live, with 95 percent confidence intervals
notes: From Tables 2 and S7 of the working paper by Scott M. Mourtgos and Ian T. Adams, posted Aug. 16, 2026: 216 agencies that adopted the cameras from 2019 to 2024, 168 of them before the crime data end, and 3,108 that did not; crime data from 2017 to 2023. The authors say the three weightings answer different questions rather than offering competing estimates of one effect.

errors.title: Three ways an alert can be wrong
errors.sub: Each measured against the total its own report gives
notes: Roseville’s cameras are Flock’s; the Story County and Los Angeles figures come from Axon readers in patrol cars. The Story County report was published by Footnote 4a, the reporting site of Have I Been Flocked, a project that describes its focus as license plate surveillance accountability.

price.title: The list price of a camera rose $500 in 2024
price.sub: Annual price per standard camera in contracts and price lists
notes: In 2019, a pilot in Greenville, S.C., paid $2,000 a year in all for 11 cameras, according to city contracts published by DeFlock SC, a group that opposes the cameras.

contracts.title: Of contracts with a known term, Dallas’s costs the most per year
contracts.sub: Contract value per year, with the total and term, from public records
notes: Values are as approved; some include video cameras, drones or gunshot sensors. Houston’s value is a ceiling, drawn as an outline. The Texas Department of Public Safety’s $26 million contract is not charted because its term was not reported.
